title: OPEC+ Set to Hold Output Steady as War Erodes Its Market Power; India Steps Up Russian ESPO Imports
subhead: Seven core OPEC+ members meet Sunday expected to keep October quotas unchanged, even as the Iran war undercuts the group's ability to move prices. Meanwhile India is quietly absorbing more Russian Far East crude as China pulls back and Hormuz stays choked.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Holds Steady as the War Erodes Its Leverage
sections.body:
OPEC+ is expected to leave its oil production policy unchanged for October when seven core members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — meet online Sunday, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing three sources. The September increase already completed the phased rollback of 1.65 million bpd of supply cuts first agreed in 2023.

But much of that added supply never reached the market. Actual production has lagged quotas as the Iran war disrupted Gulf exports through Hormuz and the Ukraine war hit Russian and Kazakh exports. OPEC output rose 1.17 million bpd in July yet stayed well below quota targets, per OilPrice.com citing Reuters. The group's production decisions now carry less weight on prices and market share than before the war, Reuters noted.

Attention is shifting to 2027 production baselines, which determine individual quotas. Dallas-based DeGolyer and MacNaughton is reviewing most members' production capacity, with findings due in late September. Iraq is pushing for a higher quota, the UAE left OPEC in May over its quota, and Venezuela is considering leaving the group.
sections.whyItMatters: The war has quietly hollowed out OPEC+'s central function — managing the market. With Gulf barrels trapped behind Hormuz, the group's quota decisions are becoming secondary to physical supply disruptions, and the 2027 baseline fight is exposing internal fractures (UAE exit, Venezuela doubts, Iraq demands).

sections.heading: Hormuz: Two Filipino Sailors Killed, Saudi Formally Accuses Iran
sections.body:
Two Filipino crew members died from Monday's attack on the Saudi oil tanker Sidr, operated by state shipping firm Bahri, Bahri confirmed Wednesday. Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry formally accused Iran of targeting the vessel and condemned attacks threatening 'the security and safety of maritime navigation and global energy supplies,' per OilPrice.com. The Sidr is the fourth Bahri vessel attacked since June.

Iran launched missiles and drones against U.S. military facilities in Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE on Wednesday after U.S. forces struck Iranian air defenses, radar, maritime assets and mine-laying capabilities a day earlier. President Trump said the U.S. now has 'almost total control of the Hormuz Strait' and warned of a response 'at a much harder and higher level' if Tehran retaliates further.

Only four commodity vessels crossed Hormuz on Tuesday, versus 10 on Monday and a 10-day average of around 13, according to preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The first confirmed deaths of tanker crew in this phase of the war sharply raise the stakes for Riyadh, which has so far avoided direct military retaliation. With transit down to four ships a day, the physical supply picture — not OPEC+ targets — is what is setting prices.

sections.heading: India Steps Up Russian ESPO Imports as China Pulls Back
sections.body:
India raised its purchases of Russia's Far East ESPO blend in the first seven months of 2026 as China backed out of the spot market early in the Iran war and Middle East deliveries slumped with the Hormuz closure, OilPrice.com reported, citing Russian daily Kommersant and Argus data. Total ESPO exports from the port of Kozmino rose 6% in January-July year on year.

China remained the key buyer but its share of Kozmino shipments fell to 83% from 88%, while India's share rose to 16% from 12%, per Vortexa and Kpler data. Analysts cited by Kommersant say India is not eating into China's share — it is absorbing volumes Chinese refiners would not buy amid slashed total crude imports. India's overall Russian crude intake eased in August from July's record high as Ukrainian attacks on Russian export infrastructure and competition from China dented deliveries.
sections.whyItMatters: The ESPO shift shows how the war is re-sorting Asian crude flows: China retreats from spot purchases, India backfills, and Russia's Pacific export route becomes a more important outlet as its western and Gulf-facing logistics are disrupted. It is a logistics-driven reshuffle, not a strategic realignment.

sections.heading: Qatar and UAE Turn to Rare LNG Ship-to-Ship Transfers
sections.body:
Three LNG carriers loaded from Qatar and the UAE transferred their cargoes onto other vessels outside the Strait of Hormuz in the past month — a highly unusual move for LNG, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing Vortexa and Kpler vessel-tracking data. The Greek-owned GasLog Shanghai, involved in a Hormuz 'incident' in late July, transferred its cargo onto GasLog Savannah offshore Oman. The Qatar-owned Al Rekayyat, hit by a projectile in early July, conducted an STS transfer with the Tembek, whose cargo reached India on August 31. ADNOC's Mraweh made an STS onto the LNG Enugu and is en route to Japan.

LNG traffic at Hormuz remains at a standstill even as oil flows have partially rebounded, because LNG is far harder to shuttle-ship and reload than crude. Qatar's extended force majeure on deliveries, combined with the U.S.-Iran re-escalation, has pushed Asia's spot LNG prices to a five-month high and Europe's benchmark gas to a three-and-a-half-year high this week.
sections.whyItMatters: Ship-to-ship transfers are a workaround, not a fix — they keep a trickle of Qatari and Emirati LNG moving but cannot restore normal volumes. The LNG market is absorbing the Hormuz blockage far worse than crude, and the price signal is now showing up in both Asia and Europe.

sections.heading: Chevron Puts a Number on Venezuela: $7 Billion, 600,000 bpd
sections.body:
Chevron will invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years and more than double its production there to about 600,000 bpd, Reuters reported Wednesday. The investment follows new agreements giving Chevron improved fiscal, commercial and legal terms plus additional Orinoco Belt acreage, including Carabobo-1 and Carabobo-2-South-A assigned to the Petroindependencia joint venture, in which Chevron holds 49%. Its three Venezuelan joint ventures have raised production 15% this year.

Chevron currently produces about 290,000 bpd in Venezuela, all exported to the U.S. Venezuela is producing roughly 1.1-1.2 million bpd, down from over 3 million bpd in the late 1990s. The investment is separate from Washington's agreement to take a majority stake in 17 oilfields holding about 65 billion barrels of proved reserves, and from Trump's call for roughly $100 billion to rebuild the industry after Maduro's removal in January. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips have yet to return after their assets were nationalized in 2007.
sections.whyItMatters: This converts the earlier 'significant size' Venezuela agreements into a concrete commercial commitment. Chevron is moving first and fast to lock in Orinoco acreage and terms before rivals return, positioning itself as the anchor of a U.S.-directed Venezuelan rebuild.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Aims to Free 1 Million bpd of Domestic Oil Burn
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia wants to displace more than 1 million bpd of domestic liquid-fuel consumption by 2030, primarily through natural gas and renewables, with nuclear playing a larger role after 2030, OilPrice.com reported, citing Arab News and IEA data. The kingdom's power stations, desalination plants, factories and farms consume over 1 million bpd of liquid fuel. A proposed 2.8-GW nuclear plant could displace the equivalent of around 105,000 bpd of crude.

On July 22, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia signed a 30-year civil nuclear cooperation agreement, clearing the way for U.S. companies to supply reactors, nuclear materials and technical services. The IEA estimates Saudi electricity demand grew 3.8% in 2025 and forecasts 3.1% average annual growth through 2030. Saudi crude and fuel-oil burn for power generation peaks in summer, reaching 1.42 million bpd in June 2024 before falling to an average of 678,000 bpd in early 2025, per EIA data.
sections.whyItMatters: Every barrel Saudi Arabia stops burning domestically is a barrel available for export — a quiet way to add supply without raising quotas. The U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal ties Riyadh's post-2030 power strategy to American suppliers, a strategic foothold that also frees more Saudi crude for the export market.

sections.heading: U.S. Army Commits $2.2 Billion to Nuclear Microreactors
sections.body:
The U.S. Army has awarded up to $2.2 billion over five years to build, own and operate commercial nuclear microreactors at five domestic military bases under its Janus Program, estimating 20 microreactors will be deployed, OilPrice.com reported, citing AP. Five vendors were selected: Antares Nuclear at Fort Bragg, BWXT at Fort Campbell, General Atomics at Fort Hood, Radiant Industries at Fort Benning and Westinghouse at Fort Drum. Radiant secured a contract worth up to $750 million to deploy 15 of its 1-MWe Kaleidos microreactors.

The military logic is that transporting fossil fuels to remote front lines creates an easy target, while localized reactors can operate for years without refueling. The push could accelerate commercial nuclear adoption as Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta pursue advanced nuclear to meet AI and data-center electricity demand.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is becoming a first-mover customer for advanced nuclear, using defense procurement to de-risk a technology the private sector is also chasing for AI power demand. It signals that energy resilience — not just cost — is now a driver of U.S. nuclear policy.

bottomLine: The dominant story today is that the Iran war is eroding the tools the market normally uses to manage supply. OPEC+ is expected to hold output steady on Sunday even as its decisions lose force behind a choked Hormuz, where transit has fallen to four ships a day and the first tanker crew deaths have drawn a formal Saudi accusation against Iran. Around the edges, the war is re-sorting flows: India is absorbing more Russian ESPO crude as China retreats, Qatar and the UAE are resorting to rare LNG ship-to-ship transfers, and Chevron has put a $7 billion, 600,000 bpd number on its Venezuela bet. Longer-term supply strategies — Saudi Arabia freeing a million bpd of domestic burn, the U.S. Army's $2.2 billion microreactor push — are moving forward in parallel, but none of them changes the immediate picture: physical Gulf supply, not policy, is setting prices.
sources: OilPrice.com (Reuters, Kommersant/Argus, Vortexa, Kpler, AP, Arab News, IEA, EIA, MEES)
